evidence.title: Banks et al., Stable added-mass partitioned FSI algorithm

records.rationale: The quasi-Newton motivation is sound, but the categorical premise that full Newton requires explicit Jacobian assembly and factorization is false without restricting the implementation. Newton-Krylov methods can use matrix-free Jacobian actions.

evidence.title: PETSc SNES nonlinear-solver manual
evidence.finding: Newton methods can use iterative and matrix-free Jacobian-vector actions. Quasi-Newton methods include limited-memory BFGS and Broyden variants; explicit assembly and direct factorization are not mandatory for Newton.
Newton solves J*delta=-F. An iterative solve only needs the action v->Jv, which may be evaluated analytically or by directional differences, without storing or directly factorizing J.
L-BFGS approximates a Hessian in optimization, or a symmetric Jacobian in suitable nonlinear formulations; it is not generally an unconstrained replacement for every nonsymmetric coupled Jacobian.

records.rationale: The nearby-divergence explanation is correct, but the unconditional claim that the function is undefined at the asymptote is false. Defining f(0)=0 and f(x)=1/x^2 otherwise leaves x=0 a vertical asymptote.

evidence.finding: Claims are checked with symbolic identities, explicit counterexamples and exact equation residuals.
Define f(x)=1/x^2 for x!=0 and f(0)=0. The line x=0 is a vertical asymptote but the graph contains (0,0). Changing one function value does not change the divergent nearby limit.
An isolated point on the line is not a continuous branch crossing it; the rejection rests on the false undefined-value requirement.

records.rationale: Correct qualitative complementarity description for contact and optimization: a positive slack/gap entails zero multiplier/normal force, while a nonzero multiplier/force entails zero slack/gap.

evidence.title: MIT nonlinear programming, constrained optimality, Theorem 11
evidence.finding: Theorem 11 on printed page 10 gives nonnegative multipliers and complementary slackness u_i*g_i=0 for inequality constraints.
With g>=0, lambda>=0 and g*lambda=0, at least one factor is zero; both may be zero at a degenerate active constraint.
This is the standard complementarity structure; it does not establish that every inequality problem has the same solver complexity.

records.rationale: Constraint drift can cause the serious failure modes listed, but growth and eventual blow-up are presented as inevitable. Small violations can remain bounded or decay depending on the equations, integrator and stabilization.

evidence.finding: A stable error equation g_dot=-g produces decaying rather than growing violations. Therefore drift outcomes depend on off-manifold dynamics and stabilization.
For g_dot=-g, a violation g(0)=epsilon evolves as epsilon*exp(-t), so small violations do not necessarily grow. This does not eliminate the need to monitor constraints.

records.rationale: Correct conceptual explanation for the ordinary nonempty real ellipse/parabola/hyperbola conics explicitly discussed: their projective completions are equivalent, while affine transformations preserve their type distinctions. The explanation does not need to classify conics over arbitrary fields.

evidence.title: Nigel Hitchin, Oxford: Quadrics
evidence.finding: Section 3.2 explicitly relates the ordinary nonempty real ellipse, parabola and hyperbola under projective completion. It separately notes that positive-definite real forms have empty projective zero sets.
A nonsingular real conic with a real point has an indefinite rank-three form. Up to nonzero scalar its signature is (2,1); Sylvester congruence takes it to x^2+y^2-z^2=0.
The claim must not be extrapolated to empty real conics or arbitrary fields. Over R, a positive-definite quadratic form has an empty projective zero set.

records.rationale: Correct outline of PID implies UFD: irreducibles generate maximal proper ideals, ACC gives existence of factorization and primality gives uniqueness.

evidence.finding: In a PID an irreducible generates a maximal proper ideal and hence is prime. ACC on principal ideals ensures irreducible factorization exists; primality yields uniqueness up to units and order.
If (p) is contained properly in (a) and p=ab with p irreducible, then a is a unit unless (a)=(p); all ideals are principal, so (p) is maximal proper.

records.rationale: Correct volume, handedness and degeneracy interpretation for an ordered set of three real vectors in the standard oriented Euclidean space.

evidence.finding: For ordered real vectors u,v,w, det[u v w]=u dot (v cross w); its absolute value is parallelepiped volume, sign is orientation and zero is linear dependence.

The scalar triple product changes sign on exchanging two vectors and vanishes exactly when they are linearly dependent, placing all three in a plane through the origin or a lower-dimensional subspace.

records.rationale: The augmented-Lagrangian steps are broadly correct, but adding a quadratic penalty does not generally improve conditioning. The advantage over a pure penalty method is that multiplier updates can achieve accuracy without forcing the penalty arbitrarily large.

evidence.title: Nick Gould, Penalty and augmented Lagrangian methods
evidence.finding: Penalty Hessians can become ill-conditioned. Augmented Lagrangian methods use multiplier updates to avoid requiring an indefinitely increasing penalty; adding a quadratic penalty does not universally improve conditioning.
For f=(x1^2+x2^2)/2 and constraint x1=0, the augmented Hessian is diag(1+rho,1), whose condition number is 1+rho, larger than the original value 1 for rho>0.

records.rationale: Correct introductory description of proving uniqueness by showing any two qualifying candidates are equal. The stated group-identity example already has existence from the group axioms; the informal opening describes unique existence rather than claiming the equality argument alone creates an object.

evidence.finding: The implication P(x) and P(y) => x=y establishes at most one solution. Existence additionally requires some x satisfying P(x). An empty solution set satisfies the implication vacuously.
For two group identities e and f, e=e*f=f. Existence is part of the group axioms.
The equality argument proves at most one; existence must be known, assumed, axiomatic or proved separately.
